concepts.title: Displacement Current
concepts.definition: Maxwell patched a hole in Ampere's loop rule by declaring that a changing electric field acts like a current: epsilon0 times the rate of change of electric flux counts alongside the wire current, so the field comes out the same for every surface spanning the loop.
concepts.key_idea: With this term the loop rule becomes the Ampere-Maxwell law, and time-varying E and B fields become mutual sources - the seed of every electromagnetic wave.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph108.txt section 8.2 (Eqs. 8.3-8.6, charging capacitor contradiction, Maxwell's equations in vacuum)
question_patterns: why does the loop rule give conflicting fields around a charging capacitor
what is displacement current and where does it flow
write the generalised ampere law including the extra term
how does a changing electric field produce a magnetic field
is there a magnetic field between capacitor plates while they charge
state the four Maxwell equations in vacuum and what each says

solution_steps.explain: a flat loop around the wire encloses current; a pot-shaped surface slipping between the plates encloses none, yet the loop field is fixed
between the plates the electric flux changes exactly as fast as the charge, so epsilon0 d(PhiE)/dt matches the wire current
adding this displacement current makes every spanning surface yield the same total current and hence the same field

concepts.title: AC Current into a Capacitor
concepts.definition: A capacitor on an alternating supply carries a steady rms conduction current V over XC in its wires; between the plates the displacement current takes over with exactly the same value, so the circuit never truly breaks.
concepts.key_idea: Kirchhoff's junction rule survives at the plates once displacement current is counted: conduction in, displacement out, equal at every instant.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph108.txt section 8.2 (Eq. 8.4 id = i, Exercise 8.1-8.2 data)
question_patterns: a 100 pF capacitor sits on a 230 V supply of angular frequency 300 rad/s; what rms current flows in the leads

solution_steps.explain: XC equals 1 over omega C
the supply voltage divided by the reactance; the same value flows as displacement current between the plates

concepts.title: How Accelerated Charges Radiate
concepts.definition: Static or steadily moving charges make steady fields only; a charge that accelerates - for instance one oscillating in an antenna or dipole - sheds electromagnetic waves whose frequency matches the oscillation.
concepts.key_idea: The radiated fields regenerate each other as they travel, and the wave energy is paid for by the source charge - which is why lab circuits reach radio frequencies long before light frequencies.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph108.txt section 8.3.1 (accelerated charge radiation, Hertz 1887, Bose, Marconi, Exercise 8.6)
question_patterns: what kind of charge motion emits electromagnetic waves

what role does an electric dipole play as a wave source

solution_steps.explain: an oscillating charge whips the local electric field up and down at its own frequency
the varying E field makes a varying B field, which makes E again, and the pair walks away through space
the wave carries the oscillator's frequency and draws its energy from the source

concepts.title: Transverse Nature of EM Waves
concepts.definition: In a plane electromagnetic wave the electric and magnetic oscillations stand at right angles to one another and to the travel direction, so the wave is transverse and can be labelled by the plane of its electric field.
concepts.formula: direction of E cross B equals the propagation direction
concepts.key_idea: Both fields rise and fall in step (in phase) as sin(kz - omega t); the cross product E x B points the way the wave travels.
question_patterns: a wave runs along z; in which directions may its E and B fields point

solution_steps.explain: take E along x and B along y for a wave moving along z, as in the standard figure
E is perpendicular to B and both are perpendicular to the travel direction
E x B lands along the propagation direction, settling which way the wave runs

concepts.title: Field Amplitudes in a Light Wave
concepts.definition: The electric and magnetic amplitudes of an electromagnetic wave lock together through the wave speed: B0 equals E0 over c, so a 6.3 V/m electric swing pairs with only about 2e-8 T of magnetic swing.
concepts.key_idea: Because c is huge, the magnetic partner of even a strong electric field is tiny in tesla - but the two fields carry equal energy on average.
question_patterns: the electric field of a wave reads 6.3 V/m at some instant; find the magnetic field then

solution_steps.explain: the amplitude ratio is fixed: B0 = E0 over c

concepts.title: Wavelength from Wave Frequency
concepts.definition: Every electromagnetic wave in vacuum runs at the same speed c, so its wavelength is simply that speed split by the frequency; a 30 MHz wave spans 10 m while a radio band of 7.5 to 12 MHz maps to roughly 40 down to 25 m.
concepts.key_idea: Frequency and wavelength trade off inversely because the speed is fixed; the product nu lambda always equals c in vacuum.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph108.txt section 8.3.2 (Eq. 8.9b nu lambda = c, Exercises 8.4-8.5, 8.10)
question_patterns: a wave oscillates at 2.0e10 Hz; what is its wavelength in vacuum

what wavelength belongs to a given broadcast frequency
how does the wavelength change when the oscillation frequency doubles

solution_steps.explain: wavelength equals c over frequency because c = nu lambda

concepts.title: Reading a Wave Expression
concepts.definition: A written field component like B0 sin(kx + omega t) is a data sheet: comparing coefficients gives the wavelength as 2 pi over k, the frequency as omega over 2 pi, and multiplying B0 by c returns the electric amplitude.
concepts.key_idea: A plus sign inside the argument means the wave travels toward negative x; the amplitudes still obey B0 = E0 over c.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph108.txt section 8.3.2 (Eq. 8.8 k = 2 pi / lambda, Example 8.2 By expression)
question_patterns: a magnetic field varies as B0 sin(0.5e3 x + 1.5e11 t); find the wavelength and frequency

solution_steps.explain: the wave number counts radians per metre, so lambda is 2 pi over k
the angular frequency is 2 pi times the ordinary frequency
multiply the magnetic amplitude by c to get E0

concepts.title: Wave Speed from EM Constants
concepts.definition: Maxwell's equations fix the wave speed as 1 over the square root of permittivity times permeability; with vacuum values this reproduces the measured speed of light, and material values give the slower speed inside media.
concepts.key_idea: Matching c to optical measurements proved light is an electromagnetic wave, and the medium's epsilon and mu set its refractive behaviour.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph108.txt section 8.3.2 (Eqs. 8.9a, 8.11, speed independence of wavelength in vacuum)
question_patterns: show that 1 over root mu0 epsilon0 equals the speed of light

solution_steps.explain: the speed depends on the product of permittivity and permeability
v equals 1 over the square root of that product

concepts.title: Bands of the EM Spectrum
concepts.definition: Electromagnetic waves span one continuous ladder from long radio waves to ultra-short gamma rays, named by wavelength and by how each band is produced or caught, with fuzzy borders and overlaps between neighbours.
concepts.formula: same vacuum speed c for every band
concepts.key_idea: Radio comes from electrons in aerials, microwaves from klystrons and magnetrons, infrared from warm matter, light and UV from atomic electron jumps, X-rays from inner-shell bombardment, gamma rays from nuclei - yet all fly at c in vacuum.
question_patterns: arrange the em spectrum bands from longest to shortest wavelength

solution_steps.explain: order the bands by wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray
each band pairs a production mechanism with its usual detector, from aerials to photographic film
wavelength and frequency differ across bands but the vacuum speed c is common to all
